My tools have proper widgets now

26 October 2026 6 min read
Software paulblish

Paulblish has let me write little web tools straight into markdown for a while: you can put some HTML and JavaScript in an html embed code block and it turns it into real html/js on the page.

That's how my air fryer converter and currency converter work. Text boxes and buttons already looked fine, but anything fancier, like a dial, a toggle or a bar chart, meant writing a pile of CSS for every single tool.

Now Paulblish ships a set of css tool widgets.

Plain form elements are styled with no classes at all, and everything else needs one class at most: knob turns a slider into a dial, segmented turns radio buttons into a button bar, switch turns a checkbox into a toggle, and bars, gauge and stats show off the results. A tiny helper script keeps the dials and live readouts in sync, so my own script only has to do the maths.

Every style has zero specificity, so a tool that wants to look different just adds its own <style>.

And it all works in any markdown file in Paulblish now, not just tools, which is how this post can show them off:

html
<input type="range" class="knob" min="40" max="220" value="96">
<label><input type="checkbox" class="switch"> Accent the first beat</label>
<dl class="bars"><dt>Wind</dt><dd style="--value: 57">57%</dd></dl>

Here are three I made for this post. A metronome for drum practice (turn your sound on, then drag the knob or click it and use the arrow keys). A race time predictor for my running. And a live look at what's powering the GB grid right now, from the same NESO API as my terminal tool.

Carbon intensity is loading, in grams of CO₂ per kWh.

Every widget, with the HTML to write for it, is on the tool widgets page. The metronome above is about 20 lines of HTML and not a single line of CSS, so the only code I have to write is the bit that goes beep.

The change is on GitHub and, as always, fork away if you want it for your own site. 🎛️
